name: Hector Salgado
equipment: Chef's cleaver, his own, wrapped in a side towel
Kitchen whites and a black skull cap, and steel-toe kitchen clogs
Two quart deli containers of rice and beans, a bag of day-old rolls and a jar of the restaurant's sofrito
A Zippo lighter (he quit smoking four years ago and kept the lighter)
Burn salve and a box of blue kitchen plasters
Union card (Local 6, Hotel and Restaurant Workers)
Keys to Osteria Sette, including the walk-in and the basement
A rubber-banded roll of the week's tips, counted into his wallet
features: Human (+1 to all six ability scores)
Hard Hitter (unarmed strikes deal 1d6 + STR bludgeoning, may use DEX instead; may make an unarmed strike as a bonus action after taking the Attack action)
Hard to Kill (when reduced to 0 HP but not killed outright, drop to 1 HP instead; once per long rest)
Union Card (Blue-Collar Worker feature: union workers — kitchen staff, porters, sanitation, building crews — will shelter him, feed him and tell him what they have seen)

personality.traits: I feed people. When it is bad I find a stove, and when there is no stove I find a cold thing that can be shared. I am big and I am quiet and I know that the quiet part is more frightening than the big part.
personality.ideals: Everybody eats. Nobody in my kitchen ever went home hungry and nobody in whatever this is going to either.
personality.bonds: My mother, Graciela, seventy-four, in a fifth-floor walk-up on 141st Street in Harlow with a bad hip and a canary. My line: Dee, Kwame, little Rafi on the dish pit, who were in the kitchen with me when it happened.
personality.flaws: I fought for money for three years when I was young and stupid, and when somebody pushes me my hands decide before I do. I have not lost my temper in eleven years, and I can feel it waiting.

appearance: A heavy-shouldered Puerto Rican man of thirty-one, six foot two, in kitchen whites gone grey at the cuffs, a black skull cap and steel-toe clogs. A burn-scar ladder up both forearms, a nose that has been broken twice and set once, and a soft, careful voice that does not go with any of it. He smells of garlic and fry oil and bleach, always, and he is the calmest person in any room until he very suddenly is not.
backstory: Hector Salgado grew up on 141st Street, fought in basements for cash from seventeen to twenty, and walked away from it the night he broke a man's jaw and did not feel anything about it. A woman named Annunziata Rocca, who ran Osteria Sette on Forty-First Street for thirty years, put him on the dish pit the following week and told him he was going to learn to make something instead. He has been her sous chef for six years and has run the line since her stroke last spring. At 4:12 on the Thursday he is prepping for a Thursday dinner service of a hundred and ten covers, with three cooks and a dishwasher and a walk-in full of food, when every burner on the line goes out at once, the ventilation hood stops, and in the silence he hears the whole of Forty-First Street hold its breath. He walks out through the dining room in his apron with the cleaver still in his hand, and the first thing he sees is a woman in a business suit walking calmly down the middle of the avenue while something fourteen feet tall walks beside her and does not look at her at all.
